```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_survival <- requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      eval = has_survival)
```

A prediction model is judged by the risks it predicts, not by its coefficients. This vignette
shows how SurvX measures the quality of predicted risks at a time horizon $t$, with one event type
and with competing risks, how it compares models fairly, and how to decide whether a model is good
enough to be used. Every measure below is computed in the C++ core of the package and has been
checked against the reference implementations (vignette 6).

The questions, and the functions that answer them:

| Question | Measure | Function |
|---|---|---|
| How close are the predicted risks to the outcomes? | Brier score, IPA | `brier_score()` |
| Do subjects with the event get higher risks? | time-dependent AUC | `auc_t()` |
| Are predicted risks of 20% right for 20% of subjects? | O/E, calibration curve, ICI, E50, E90 | `calibration()` |
| Does the score rank subjects over the whole follow-up? | concordance index C | `cindex()` |
| Which of several models predicts best, and is the difference real? | all of the above, cross-validated, with paired tests | `compare_models()`, `cv_compare()`, `model_scan()` |
| Would deciding by the model do more good than harm? | net benefit | `decision_curve()` |
| Does a covariate add to a nested model? | likelihood-ratio test | `anova()` |

## 1. Data and two models

We use the `lung` data of **survival** and predict death within one year.

```{r}
library(SurvX)
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1
lung$years <- lung$time / 365.25
lung <- lung[stats::complete.cases(lung[, c("years", "status", "age", "sex", "ph.ecog")]), ]
f_small <- cox(Event(years, status) ~ age + sex, lung)
f_big <- cox(Event(years, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, lung)
r_small <- 1 - predict(f_small, lung, times = 1, type = "survival")[, 1]
r_big <- 1 - predict(f_big, lung, times = 1, type = "survival")[, 1]
summary(r_big)
```

## 2. Overall accuracy: the Brier score and IPA

The Brier score is the mean squared difference between the predicted risk and the outcome by $t$
(1 if the event happened, 0 if not), with inverse probability of censoring weights so that
censored subjects are accounted for (Graf et al. 1999; Gerds & Schumacher 2006). It measures
calibration and discrimination together. On its own it is hard to read, because it depends on how
common the event is; the index of prediction accuracy (IPA) compares it with a model that gives
everybody the same risk, the Kaplan-Meier (with competing risks Aalen-Johansen) estimate
(Kattan & Gerds 2018).

```{r}
brier_score(lung$years, lung$status, r_big, t = 1, se = TRUE)
```

* `brier` 0 is perfect; predicting 50% for everybody scores 0.25.
* `ipa` 0.10 means the model removes 10% of the error of the model without covariates; a negative
  IPA means the model is worse than no model.
* `se` is the standard error from the influence function of the Brier score, with the censoring
  weights taken as known: the "conservative" standard error of `riskRegression::Score`.

## 3. Discrimination: the AUC at the horizon

The time-dependent AUC is the probability that a subject with the event by $t$ has a higher
predicted risk than a subject without it (Blanche et al. 2013). With competing risks, subjects
who failed from another cause count as controls. 0.5 is no discrimination, 1 is perfect.

```{r}
auc_t(lung$years, lung$status, r_big, t = 1, se = TRUE)
```

The AUC ignores calibration: multiplying every risk by two leaves it unchanged. It must always be
read together with a calibration measure.

## 4. Calibration

Calibration asks whether the predicted risks come true. `calibration()` gives three views:

* **in risk groups**: the mean predicted against the observed (Kaplan-Meier or Aalen-Johansen)
  risk in groups of predicted risk (Gerds, Andersen & Kattan 2014), and their size-weighted
  absolute difference, the calibration error;
* **in the large**: the observed over the expected (mean predicted) number of events, O/E, with
  its interval; O/E = 1.2 means the model predicts 20% too few events;
* **smooth**: a calibration curve from a Cox model (with competing risks, a Fine-Gray model) of
  the outcome on a natural spline of $\log\{-\log(1 - \hat r)\}$, and the integrated calibration
  index ICI, the mean absolute difference between predicted and calibrated risks, with its median
  E50 and 90th percentile E90 (Austin, Harrell & van Klaveren 2020).

```{r}
cal <- calibration(lung$years, lung$status, r_big, t = 1, groups = 5)
cal
attr(cal, "oe")                                         # O/E and its interval
c(ICI = attr(cal, "ici"), E50 = attr(cal, "e50"), E90 = attr(cal, "e90"))
```

```{r calibration-plot, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 5}
sm <- attr(cal, "smooth")
plot(cal$predicted, cal$observed, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), pch = 19,
     xlab = "predicted 1-year risk", ylab = "observed 1-year risk")
lines(sm$predicted, sm$observed, col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

Points and curve close to the diagonal and an ICI of a few hundredths mean good calibration.

## 5. The concordance index, and why it is not used to compare models

The C index (Harrell et al. 1982) is the share of comparable pairs in which the subject who had the
event first has the higher score. It describes ranking over the whole follow-up and is the usual
summary of a Cox model; it is printed by `summary()` of Cox, cause-specific Cox and parametric
models. Uno's version weights the pairs by the inverse probability of censoring so that it does not
depend on the censoring distribution (Uno et al. 2011); restrict it to a time `tau` where
follow-up is still adequate. With competing risks, `cindex()` gives the C index of one cause of
Wolbers et al. (2009), and with `method = "uno"` its weighted version (Wolbers et al. 2014); without
competing events these are exactly Harrell's and Uno's indices.

```{r}
cindex(f_big)
cindex(f_big, method = "uno", tau = 2)
```

For predicted risks at a time horizon the C index is not a proper measure: a model with the wrong
risks can have a higher C than the true model (Blanche, Kattan & Gerds 2019). This is why the
comparison tables of SurvX report the AUC at the horizon and the Brier score, and not C.

## 6. Comparing models: paired differences and cross-validation

Measured on the data used for fitting, every measure is optimistic, more so for larger models.
`cv_compare()` fits any list of models in K-fold cross-validation, pools the out-of-fold
predictions and computes every measure from them; `compare_models()` does the same in the C++ core
for the direct, Fine-Gray and cause-specific models. The same folds are used for every model, so the
comparison is paired: for each model the table gives its difference from the model with the lowest
Brier score at that time, with the standard error of the paired difference (from the difference of
the influence functions on the same subjects) and a p-value.

```{r}
cc <- cv_compare(Event(years, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, lung, times = c(0.5, 1), folds = 5,
                 models = list("age + sex" = function(f, d) cox(Event(years, status) ~ age + sex, d),
                               "age + sex + ph.ecog" = function(f, d) cox(f, d)))
cc
```

```{r cv-plot}
plot(cc, measure = "brier")
```

The columns of `as.data.frame(cc)` ending in `_cv` are cross-validated. Besides the Brier score,
IPA, AUC and calibration error they include their standard errors and 95% intervals
(`brier_se_cv`, `auc_lower_cv`, ...), the O/E with its interval, ICI, E50, E90 and the paired
differences (`brier_diff_cv`, `brier_diff_p_cv`, `auc_diff_cv`, ...). A difference whose interval
excludes zero is a real difference on these data; a difference in the third decimal of the Brier
score with a large p-value is noise, and the simpler model should be preferred.

With competing risks the same applies to the risk of one cause:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
n <- 400
d <- data.frame(x = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), z = rnorm(n))
t1 <- rexp(n, 0.4 * exp(0.6 * d$x + 0.4 * d$z)); t2 <- rexp(n, 0.3); cens <- runif(n, 0, 4)
d$time <- pmin(t1, t2, cens)
d$status <- ifelse(d$time == cens, 0, ifelse(t1 < t2, 1, 2))
cm <- compare_models(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, times = 2, folds = 3,
                     direct = list(c("gompertz", "PH")))
cm
```

`model_scan()` goes one step further: it fits every model of the package that suits the data,
ranks them by the cross-validated integrated Brier score with the one-standard-error rule, and adds
the time-averaged AUC over the follow-up (`iauc_cv`) and the mean ICI (`ici_cv`) to its table.

## 7. Is the model useful? Decision curves

Good accuracy does not by itself mean that deciding by the model helps. Decision curve analysis
(Vickers & Elkin 2006) asks: if everybody with a predicted risk of at least $p$ were treated, would
the true positives outweigh the false positives, each false positive weighted by the odds
$p/(1-p)$ that a decision maker accepts at threshold $p$? With censored data the true positives are
estimated by the Kaplan-Meier (Aalen-Johansen) risk among the subjects above the threshold
(Vickers et al. 2008).

```{r}
dc <- decision_curve(list("age + sex" = r_small, "age + sex + ph.ecog" = r_big),
                     lung$years, lung$status, t = 1, thresholds = seq(0.2, 0.8, by = 0.02))
dc
```

```{r decision-plot}
plot(dc)
```

A model is useful at a threshold where its net benefit is above both "treat all" and "treat none".
Look only at the thresholds that matter for the decision.

## 8. Nested models: likelihood-ratio tests

When the question is whether a covariate adds information, a likelihood-ratio test of nested models
answers it directly:

```{r}
anova(f_small, f_big)
```

The test uses the partial likelihood for Cox models (as `survival::anova.coxph`) and the full
likelihood for parametric, cure, frailty and joint or constrained direct models. Fine-Gray and
weighted direct models maximise pseudo-likelihoods; for them `anova()` refuses and the Wald tests of
`summary()` should be used.

## 9. What to report

For a prediction model, report at the horizons of interest (Collins et al. 2015, TRIPOD):

1. the Brier score with IPA, and the AUC, each with its interval, cross-validated or on external data;
2. calibration: O/E with its interval, the calibration plot and ICI;
3. for a comparison, the paired differences from the reference model with their intervals;
4. for a model meant to guide decisions, the decision curve over the relevant thresholds.

`sx_references("cindex")`, `sx_references("calibration")`, `sx_references("compare_models")` and
`sx_references("decision_curve")` print the full references of every method used.
